counterexample_without_separation.space: Theta={0,1,2}, full sigma-algebra; identical clean laws on one-point sample space, N>=1.
counterexample_without_separation.clean_premise: At threshold M0=b every action has loss>=b for at least two of the three targets. All targets have identical data law, so summing the three tail probabilities is at least2; their maximum is at least2/3, hence the premise holds with c0=1/2 even for randomized estimators.
counterexample_without_separation.failure: All pairs have TV0 and omega=M. The constant action2 has loss at most b under every target and contaminant. Thus its tail risk is0 at every threshold>b. Taking M arbitrarily large contradicts any positive universal threshold multiple of max(M0,omega) without loss-separation control. Identically-zero loss is not used as a counterexample because its modulus is0.

mathematical_arguments.orientation: Actual def-loss-function-and-risk is target-first L(theta,a). Current robust-risk and modulus definitions already retain this convention. For asymmetric losses L(theta0,theta1) regards theta1 as action; the ordered pair sup and separation are retained, rather than assuming symmetry.
mathematical_arguments.asymmetric_scope: For metric d and weights0<m<=w(theta)<=B, L(theta,a)=w(theta)d(theta,a) satisfies separation with kappa=m/(2B), allowing asymmetric losses.
mathematical_arguments.equalization: Let delta=TV(P0,P1) under event-supremum convention. Against nu=P0+P1, both positive and negative parts of p0-p1 integrate to delta. Normalizing these parts gives Q0,Q1 equalizing at epsilon_prime=delta/(1+delta). For epsilon>=epsilon_prime, mix each Qi with Pi using weight epsilon_prime/epsilon. Epsilon0 requires delta0 and identical laws; epsilon1 uses any common contaminant. This proves the exact threshold delta<=epsilon/(1-epsilon) without mutual domination of the two clean laws.
mathematical_arguments.tail_constant: For omega<=M0, Q=Ptheta embeds the clean law and kappa M0/4<=M0. For finite omega>M0, a pair has separation>omega/2; equalization yields a common iid sample law and pointwise loss separation>=kappa Lpair>kappa omega/2. Two measurable events cover that law, so one has probability>=1/2 at threshold kappa omega/4. Taking worst-case sup then estimator inf gives min(c0,1/2). The argument does not assume attainment of omega. Infinite omega supplies a pair beyond any finite threshold.
mathematical_arguments.bernoulli: TV(Bern(theta0),Bern(theta1))=|theta0-theta1|; absolute loss gives modulus min(epsilon/(1-epsilon),1), and omega(1)=1. For0<epsilon<=1/2, theta0=0,theta1=epsilon/(1-epsilon),Q0=delta1,Q1=delta0 give common Bern(epsilon). For epsilon>=1/2, contaminant success probabilities1/(2epsilon),1-1/(2epsilon) give Bern(1/2), including epsilon1.
